1	---
2	type: research-report
3	id: product-designer-role-2026-08
4	status: draft
5	version: 4
6	date: 2026-08-25
7	question: "Research a product designer role, which is a gap in this system: the user experience has been left to the PO, architect and the authority, and no role makes it consistent; the product has been CLI-focused but the system must handle the full range of user interaction types."
8	requested-by: product-authority
9	created: 2026-08-25
10	updated: 2026-08-25
11	---
12	
13	# Research report: the product designer role and consistency across every interaction type
14	
15	## Executive summary
16	
17	*How to read the labels.* Each finding carries a confidence: **high** —
18	several sources opened in full agree, at least one primary (the
19	standard, framework, or author itself); **medium** — one opened source,
20	or secondary accounts only (including a paywalled primary carried by an
21	opened secondary); **low** — recall without a source. "Several" means
22	two or more. "Secondhand" marks a quote taken from a
23	secondary account because the primary was unreachable. Confidence is
24	about the evidence; where a finding predicts an outcome, its likelihood
25	is stated in its own phrase.
26	
27	*How the sources' vocabulary maps to the shop.* Cagan's "Product Lead
28	Engineer" (the engineer who owns feasibility in his four-risks model) is
29	`lead-solutions-architect`; "the team" and "engineers" are
30	the Bounded Context shops (the shops that each own one Bounded Context,
31	a designed region of the product); an *interaction type* is one way a
32	person or an agent reaches the product — command line (CLI), full-screen
33	terminal (TUI), graphical or web (GUI), API and SDK, conversational
34	(chat), voice, and generated documents or notifications; a *design
35	system* is a governed set of reusable patterns, components, and rules
36	with a named owner; a *scenario* is an acceptance scenario held by a
37	Bounded Context shop's scenario register; a *clarify* is a shop's typed
38	question back to the lead shop. Abbreviations: NN/g — Nielsen Norman
39	Group; SFIA — the Skills Framework for the Information Age, whose level
40	5 is "ensure, advise"; WCAG — the W3C Web Content Accessibility
41	Guidelines, WCAG2ICT its non-web application; AIP — Google's API
42	Improvement Proposals; RACI — the responsibility matrix in which exactly
43	one party is Accountable; HAX — Microsoft's Human-AI Experience toolkit,
44	whose 18 Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction are meant throughout;
45	Grice's Cooperative Principle and "Grice's maxims" name the same
46	linguistic standard.
47	
48	1. **The gap is real and has a name: design by committee.** The shop's
49	   present state — experience decided jointly by PO, architect, and
50	   authority, no single owner — is the textbook definition — ProductPlan: "Design by committee is what
51	   happens when multiple parties are involved in the product design
52	   process, and all of their input is treated equally" — and every
53	   opened model that names the PM's peers gives usability its own owner: Cagan's
54	   four risks ("The Product Designer is responsible for the usability
55	   risk, and overall accountable for the product's experience — every
56	   interaction our users and customers have with our product"), Torres's
57	   product trio (PM, designer, engineer — "the three roles that — at a
58	   minimum — are required"). The remedy both design-by-committee sources
59	   (Dovetail; ProductPlan) give is one decision-maker deciding on
60	   evidence. *(High.)*
61	2. **The role's scope is medium-neutral by definition, so CLI, API, and
62	   agent interfaces are inside it.** UX "encompasses all aspects of the
63	   end-user's interaction" (Norman & Nielsen); interaction design is "the
64	   conversation between the user and the system" (Cagan & Baxley 2025);
65	   SFIA's user-experience analysis skill (UNAN) covers "a full range of
66	   user tasks not just digital tasks". The CLI guidance corpus (clig.dev, Heroku, GitHub's
67	   Primer CLI) is design guidance in its own right — GitHub files its CLI
68	   design under its design system. *(High.)*
69	3. **What carries consistency across interaction types is not a
70	   component library — it is a small set of governed instruments:**
71	   design principles as decision rules (NN/g, GOV.UK's "consistent, not
72	   uniform"), one vocabulary and voice (Primer "Make it feel like GitHub";
73	   NN/g tone dimensions; the GOV.UK style guide), one core task set that
74	   every interaction type supports (NN/g omnichannel; Google's
75	   conversation design; Alexa "voice-first, but not voice-only"), an
76	   accessibility standard as a cross-cutting constraint (WCAG 2.2 AA;
77	   WCAG2ICT for non-web), and per-interaction-type conventions honoured
78	   as *external* consistency (NN/g usability heuristic 4, "consistency and standards"; clig.dev "the terminal's
79	   conventions are hardwired into our fingers"). Every mature example
80	   governs these with the same form: criteria + a review body + an
81	   approval state (GOV.UK contribution criteria; Google AIP editors;
82	   Azure's stewardship board). *(High.)*
83	4. **Conversational and agent interfaces have an established external
84	   check and a real paradigm difference.** Microsoft's 18 Guidelines for
85	   Human-AI Interaction are modality-independent; Google's conversation
86	   design rests on Grice's Cooperative Principle; Nielsen classes CLI and
87	   GUI together as command-based and conversational/agent as intent-based
88	   with "reversed locus of control", and expects hybrids. The designer's
89	   consistency task therefore spans two paradigms, and for generated
90	   interfaces the designer's output becomes "guidance and constraints",
91	   not screens. *(High for the guidance; medium for the paradigm claim,
92	   one author.)*
93	5. **The agent is also a user.** NN/g: "'user' is no longer synonymous
94	   with 'human'"; Anthropic: invest in the agent-computer interface "just
95	   as much effort" as HCI. Accessibility structure (semantic names,
96	   predictable patterns) and tool/API definitions are the agent's
97	   interface — so API/SDK ergonomics and agent tool contracts sit in the
98	   designer's consistency remit, with the architect owning the contract
99	   itself. *(High — two primary sources opened in full agree; both are
100	   recent, so the practice they describe is young.)*
101	6. **The contested boundary with the PM is known and must be allocated
102	   explicitly.** NN/g's 2021 survey: PMs and UX disagree most on who owns
103	   discovery research (19% of PMs vs 73% of UX say UX), ideation,
104	   information architecture, task flows, the research agenda, and who
105	   explains design to leadership. The recorded failure modes: PMs
106	   "dictate design by sending wireframes to product designers and asking
107	   them to polish them"; the designer as decorator ("pixel-pusher");
108	   hand-off leaving the designer to find requirement gaps. *(High.)*
109	7. **The proposal for `lead-product-designer`** — composed from findings
110	   1–6, a proposal not a finding, so no confidence label; written to the
111	   six-section role form used by `researcher` and
112	   `lead-solutions-architect` — posture; decision rights (decides,
113	   recommends, escalates, never decides); admissible evidence;
114	   interfaces; knowledge and skills; anti-rationalization. *Posture:* one experience across every
115	   interaction type; evidence from users, never opinion; consistent, not
116	   uniform. *Decides (exclusive domain):* the experience guidance corpus
117	   — design principles, vocabulary and voice, the core-task parity rule,
118	   interaction patterns per interaction type, the accessibility target —
119	   and whether a delivered interaction conforms to it. *Decides:* which
120	   interaction type a capability is offered through first — an
121	   experience call, since the PM has already decided the capability is
122	   worth having and the question left is how people reach it; the
123	   information architecture and task flows of every interaction type;
124	   what user research is run and how usability is evaluated. *Recommends:*
125	   to the PM, opportunities and usability findings that change value
126	   judgments; to the PO, acceptance scenarios' usability criteria and
127	   the scenarios that a usability test invalidates; to the architect, the
128	   ergonomics of contracts, CLIs, and agent tool definitions.
129	   *Escalates:* to the authority, a principle the experience corpus cannot
130	   satisfy alongside the architecture principles, and any conflict where
131	   value (PM) and usability pull apart after re-framing. *Never decides:*
132	   what problem is worth solving (PM), acceptance (PO), the stack and
133	   contracts (architect), how a Bounded Context builds a behavior (the
134	   shop). *Admissible evidence:* user tests and trials, prototypes tested
135	   with users, expert review against the corpus, context-of-use analysis,
136	   measured task completion; not admissible — a stakeholder's preference,
137	   a PM-supplied wireframe as a requirement, the designer's own taste
138	   unrecorded. *Interfaces:* PM — framed problems and outcomes in;
139	   usability findings, prototypes, and opportunity evidence out, in
140	   discovery not after it; PO — scenarios in for usability criteria;
141	   usability acceptance criteria and test results out; architect —
142	   contract, CLI, and tool ergonomics reviewed against the corpus;
143	   feasibility and non-functional constraints in; Bounded Context shops —
144	   the corpus and its patterns out; conformance findings back; a
145	   `clarify` on experience questions answered. *Knowledge and skills* and *anti-rationalization* are set out in full
146	   under "What this means" below.
147	8. **Two decisions the sources leave to the authority.** (a) Whether the
148	   experience guidance corpus is a new definition type or a principle
149	   set plus guidelines in the existing chain form — the governance
150	   examples fit the existing form. (b) Torres puts usability on the
151	   whole trio ("The trio is jointly responsible for building a
152	   desirable, viable, feasible, usable, ethical product"); Cagan on the
153	   designer alone; the proposal follows Cagan
154	   and RACI (one accountable) with joint discovery. *(Judgment.)*
155	
156	## Method
157	
158	Three parallel gather workers in fresh contexts covered: the role's
159	definition and interfaces (Cagan/SVPG six essays, Torres two, NN/g
160	seven, SFIA 9 four skills, practitioner sources on failure modes);
161	consistency mechanisms and CLI/API design (NN/g five, GOV.UK four,
162	Atlassian three, W3C two, clig.dev, Heroku, 12-factor CLI via mirror,
163	GitHub Primer CLI via repository source, Docker, Google AIP, Azure
164	guidelines, Stripe two, Textual — a terminal-UI framework's theming guide, the only
165	TUI design document found); conversational and agent interfaces
166	(Google conversation design three pages, Microsoft HAX, NN/g five,
167	Apple WWDC transcript, Alexa two, Google's People + AI Research (PAIR) guidebook two chapters, Shneiderman, Anthropic,
168	OpenAI). About 55 sources opened in full; unreadable: ISO 9241-210
169	(paywalled — principles from a secondary), Material Design 3
170	(JavaScript-rendered), NN/g "UX vs product designer", Apple HIG Siri
171	page (substituted by Apple's own WWDC20 transcript), Amershi et al. full
172	paper (abstract and Microsoft's library used), GOV.UK working-group page
173	(410; Home Office analogue opened). Evidence extracted quotes-first;
174	synthesis; an independent fresh-context verification pass followed.
175	
176	## Findings
177	
178	### F1 — The gap and its name *(high)*
179	
180	- Cagan, "The Four Big Risks" (svpg.com/four-big-risks): "The Product
181	  Designer is responsible for the usability risk, and overall accountable
182	  for the product's experience – every interaction our users and
183	  customers have with our product." PM: "value and viability risks";
184	  engineer: "feasibility risk".
185	- Torres, "Core Concept: The Product Trio" (producttalk.org): "A product
186	  trio is typically comprised of a product manager, a designer, and a
187	  software engineer. These are the three roles that—at a minimum—are
188	  required to create good digital products."
189	- Torres, "Product Trios" (2024): "The trio is jointly responsible for
190	  building a desirable, viable, feasible, usable, ethical product."
191	- ProductPlan, "How to Avoid Design by Committee": "Design by committee
192	  is what happens when multiple parties are involved in the product
193	  design process, and all of their input is treated equally."
194	- Dovetail, "Design By Committee": "a group of designers, stakeholders,
195	  and clients working on the same project and sharing equally valid
196	  opinions"; "In product design, it usually produces low-quality
197	  results"; "you should only have one decision-maker". Riddle and
198	  Treder (UXPin), quoted by ProductPlan: "Committee design is not
199	  collaborative. It's a dictatorship of many".
200	- NN/g RACI (Kaley 2022): "For each task, there should be only one
201	  accountable person."
202	- Cagan 2006, on the absence: "Sometimes the product managers waded into
203	  the design waters and did what they could."
204	
205	### F2 — Scope is medium-neutral *(high)*
206	
207	- Norman & Nielsen, "The Definition of User Experience": "'User
208	  experience' encompasses all aspects of the end-user's interaction with
209	  the company, its services, and its products"; UX ⊃ UI ⊃ usability
210	  ("usability... is a quality attribute of the UI").
211	- Cagan & Baxley 2025: "The product designer is fundamentally responsible
212	  for the user experience of the product. The scope of that
213	  responsibility encompasses the full suite of interactions, touchpoints,
214	  and visual representations — both online and offline";
215	  "Interaction design is the practice of creating and choreographing the
216	  conversation between the user and the system."
217	- SFIA 9 UNAN: "This skill is inclusive of a full range of user tasks not
218	  just digital tasks."
219	- clig.dev: "If a command is going to be used primarily by humans, it
220	  should be designed for humans first"; "The original Macintosh Human
221	  Interface Guidelines recommend 'See-and-point (instead of
222	  remember-and-type)'... These things needn't be mutually exclusive."
223	- Heroku CLI style guide: "The primary goal of anyone developing CLI
224	  plugins should always be usability."
225	- GitHub Primer CLI (repository primer/cli, archived 2024, now under
226	  primer.style/design): "Command line interfaces are not as visually
227	  intuitive as graphical interfaces. They have very few affordances...
228	  We do our best to design our commands to mitigate this."
229	- Stripe (Bu 2020): "Keeping things simple means making sure your APIs
230	  are consistent and predictable"; "creating the right packages to
231	  gradually reveal the power of your API as your users need it."
232	
233	### F3 — What carries consistency, and how it is governed *(high)*
234	
235	- NN/g, Design Principles (Rosala): "Product design principles are value
236	  statements that describe the most important goals that a product or
237	  service should deliver for users and are used to frame design
238	  decisions."; "These principles support consistency in the way
239	  decisions are being made across teams, build confidence in the
240	  decision, and eliminate fruitless debates."; "Be careful that your
241	  principles don't conflict."
242	- GOV.UK Design Principles #9: "Be consistent, not uniform... We should
243	  use the same language and the same design patterns wherever possible.
244	  This isn't a straitjacket or a rule book." #7: "We're not designing for
245	  a screen, we're designing for people."
246	- NN/g heuristic 4: "Systems should adhere to both internal and external
247	  consistency — they should use the same patterns everywhere inside the
248	  system and should also follow web-, platform-, and domain-specific
249	  conventions." clig.dev: "The terminal's conventions are hardwired into
250	  our fingers... that's what makes CLIs intuitive and guessable".
251	- Primer CLI, "Make it feel like GitHub": "Using this tool, it should be
252	  obvious that it's GitHub and not anything else... reflect the
253	  GitHub.com interface as much as possible and appropriate"; "Language
254	  is the most important tool at our disposal for creating a clear,
255	  understandable product."
256	- NN/g tone of voice: "Keep your brand personality consistent, but vary
257	  the tone"; "used when creating writing and other communications for
258	  all channels."
259	- NN/g omnichannel: "Your channel experiences should at minimum support
260	  these core tasks on every channel"; "it's vital... to understand when
261	  it's okay to compromise consistency in order to provide an
262	  appropriately optimized experience on each channel."
263	- Atlassian: "Design tokens are the single source of truth to name and
264	  store decisions about the user interface."
265	- W3C: WCAG 2.2 "is an approved... ISO standard: ISO/IEC 40500:2025";
266	  "can also be applied to non-web information and communications
267	  technologies"; WCAG2ICT "is not a standard, so it is not possible to
268	  conform to WCAG2ICT".
269	- Governance form — GOV.UK contribution criteria: "tested in user
270	  research and shown to work with a representative sample of users,
271	  including those with disabilities"; "it has a clear owner". Google
272	  AIP-1: "Two AIP approvers (other than the author) must provide formal
273	  signoff"; AIPs "are used by API reviewers as a basis for review
274	  comments." Azure guidelines: "If you feel you need an exception,
275	  contact the Azure HTTP/REST Stewardship Board prior to
276	  implementation." NN/g Design Systems 101: "A design system is only as
277	  effective as the team that manages it."
278	
279	### F4 — Conversational and agent interfaces *(high for guidance; medium for the paradigm claim)*
280	
281	- Google conversation design (the pages carry a notice that
282	  "Conversational Actions were deprecated on June 13, 2023"; the design
283	  guidance outlives the retired product): "a breadth of design expertise (for
284	  example, voice user interface design, interaction design, visual
285	  design, motion design, and UX writing) that we've refined into a
286	  single discipline"; rests on "Grice's Maxims"; cross-modality rule:
287	  start with the spoken prompt, "condense it to create the display
288	  prompt", "they should still convey the same core message".
289	- Alexa: "A great Alexa experience is voice-first, but not voice-only";
290	  "Each touch (or remote) target on screen should have a voice command
291	  analog".
292	- Microsoft HAX, 18 guidelines (e.g. G1 "Make clear what the system can
293	  do", G9 "Support efficient correction", G11 "Make clear why the system
294	  did what it did", G17 "Provide global controls"); Amershi et al., CHI
295	  2019, DOI 10.1145/3290605.3300233 (abstract only).
296	- Nielsen, "AI: First New UI Paradigm in 60 Years": "In command-based
297	  interactions, the user issues commands to the computer one at a
298	  time"; generative AI "completely reverses the locus of control";
299	  "Future AI systems will likely have a hybrid user interface".
300	- NN/g, Generative UI: "We must guide the generative UIs, even if we
301	  aren't making minute decisions about individual components."
302	- PAIR: "your users will definitely need a manual failsafe"; AI adds
303	  "context errors" and "background errors". Shneiderman: "high levels of
304	  human control AND high levels of automation."
305	
306	### F5 — The agent as a user *(high)*
307	
308	- NN/g, "AI Agents as Users": "'user' is no longer synonymous with
309	  'human.'"; "Accessibility guidelines achieve this design goal: clear,
310	  descriptive element names, predictable interaction patterns".
311	- Anthropic, "Building effective agents": "plan to invest just as much
312	  effort in creating good agent-computer interfaces (ACI)" as HCI; "Tool
313	  definitions and specifications should be given just as much prompt
314	  engineering attention as your overall prompts."
315	
316	### F6 — The PM boundary and failure modes *(high)*
317	
318	- NN/g, Pernice & Budiu 2021: discovery research — 19% of PMs vs 73% of
319	  UX say UX owns it; IA — "75% of the UXers" say UX, "50% of product
320	  managers" say development; deciding what UX researches — "a clear
321	  example of appropriation".
322	- NN/g, PM archetype 2023: PMs "might try to dictate design by sending
323	  wireframes to product designers and asking them to polish them".
324	- Balsamiq (a wireframing vendor) dissents: "product managers can and
325	  should wireframe" — vendor interest noted; it still proposes a
326	  "Wireframes Contract" under which the PM does not dictate final design.
327	- Marvel (Veen quoted): "Good design isn't [decoration]. Good design is
328	  problem solving."
329	- Torres 2024: "A product manager hands off requirements to a designer.
330	  The designer uncovers gaps in the requirements."
331	- Cagan 2016: designers participate "in all phases of a product, from
332	  discovery to delivery"; "Good product designers use prototypes as
333	  their primary canvas"; "constantly testing their ideas with real
334	  users".
335	- SFIA 9 level 5 (lead level): UNAN "Determines the approaches to be
336	  used for user experience analysis"; USEV "Manages user experience
337	  evaluation... Advises on what to evaluate"; HCEV "Plans and drives user
338	  experience design activities."
339	
340	## What this means — the role proposal in full
341	
342	The executive summary's item 7 carries posture, decision rights,
343	evidence, and interfaces; the two remaining sections of the form live
344	here only.
345	
346	**Knowledge and skills.** SFIA 9 UNAN, HCEV, USEV, URCH at level 5
347	("ensure, advise"); the ISO 9241-210 activities (context of use, user
348	requirements, design solutions, evaluation — secondhand); the HAX
349	guidelines for any agent-facing interaction; WCAG 2.2 AA and WCAG2ICT;
350	clig.dev and Heroku conventions for CLI; Grice's maxims for
351	conversation; the shop's architecture principles (local-comprehension,
352	knowable-shape) as they bear on interfaces.
353	
354	**Anti-rationalization.** "It's a CLI, developers don't need design" —
355	clig.dev and GitHub say otherwise. "Consistency later" — GOV.UK's
356	contribution criteria gate at publication. "The PM already sketched it"
357	— NN/g's named failure mode. "An agent doesn't care" — NN/g and
358	Anthropic say the agent is a user. "It looks fine to me" — the
359	designer's own preference is not admissible evidence.
360	
361	## Alternatives considered
362	
363	- **Give usability to `lead-pm`.** Cagan's own PM definition excludes
364	  it; NN/g's survey shows the appropriation this produces. Rejected.
365	- **Give it to `lead-po` as acceptance criteria.** Acceptance is a
366	  check, not a definition of good; the check would sit with the same
367	  role that wrote the criteria. Rejected under `define-good-up-front`.
368	- **A per-interaction-type designer (CLI designer, conversation
369	  designer).** Google folded VUI/IxD/visual/writing "into a single
370	  discipline"; the consistency instruments are cross-type. Rejected;
371	  interaction-type conventions become sections of the corpus.
372	- **A design system as a component library first.** No opened source
373	  claims a component library spans CLI/GUI/API; the sources put
374	  principles, vocabulary, and governance first. Deferred.
375	- **Torres's joint accountability for usability.** Compatible in
376	  discovery; RACI and Cagan still require one accountable. The proposal
377	  keeps joint discovery and single accountability.
378	
379	## Limitations
380	
381	- ISO 9241-210 was not opened (paywalled); its principles are from an
382	  opened secondary and carry medium confidence under the scheme.
383	- No authoritative TUI design guideline exists; TUI guidance would be
384	  derived from clig.dev, WCAG2ICT, and keyboard-first GUI patterns.
385	- The empirical base for failure modes is practitioner writing and one
386	  NN/g survey; no controlled study was found.
387	- "Design theater" as a named failure mode has no primary source and is
388	  not used.
389	- The paradigm-shift claim (F4) rests on one author.
390	- What would change the judgment: a source showing a single component
391	  library successfully spanning CLI, GUI, and API; evidence that
392	  designer-owned corpora slow small teams more than committee decisions
393	  cost them.

# Research report: the product designer role and consistency across every interaction type

## Executive summary

*How to read the labels.* Each finding carries a confidence: **high** —
several sources opened in full agree, at least one primary (the
standard, framework, or author itself); **medium** — one opened source,
or secondary accounts only (including a paywalled primary carried by an
opened secondary); **low** — recall without a source. "Several" means
two or more. "Secondhand" marks a quote taken from a
secondary account because the primary was unreachable. Confidence is
about the evidence; where a finding predicts an outcome, its likelihood
is stated in its own phrase.

*How the sources' vocabulary maps to the shop.* Cagan's "Product Lead
Engineer" (the engineer who owns feasibility in his four-risks model) is
`lead-solutions-architect`; "the team" and "engineers" are
the Bounded Context shops (the shops that each own one Bounded Context,
a designed region of the product); an *interaction type* is one way a
person or an agent reaches the product — command line (CLI), full-screen
terminal (TUI), graphical or web (GUI), API and SDK, conversational
(chat), voice, and generated documents or notifications; a *design
system* is a governed set of reusable patterns, components, and rules
with a named owner; a *scenario* is an acceptance scenario held by a
Bounded Context shop's scenario register; a *clarify* is a shop's typed
question back to the lead shop. Abbreviations: NN/g — Nielsen Norman
Group; SFIA — the Skills Framework for the Information Age, whose level
5 is "ensure, advise"; WCAG — the W3C Web Content Accessibility
Guidelines, WCAG2ICT its non-web application; AIP — Google's API
Improvement Proposals; RACI — the responsibility matrix in which exactly
one party is Accountable; HAX — Microsoft's Human-AI Experience toolkit,
whose 18 Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction are meant throughout;
Grice's Cooperative Principle and "Grice's maxims" name the same
linguistic standard.

1. **The gap is real and has a name: design by committee.** The shop's
   present state — experience decided jointly by PO, architect, and
   authority, no single owner — is the textbook definition — ProductPlan: "Design by committee is what
   happens when multiple parties are involved in the product design
   process, and all of their input is treated equally" — and every
   opened model that names the PM's peers gives usability its own owner: Cagan's
   four risks ("The Product Designer is responsible for the usability
   risk, and overall accountable for the product's experience — every
   interaction our users and customers have with our product"), Torres's
   product trio (PM, designer, engineer — "the three roles that — at a
   minimum — are required"). The remedy both design-by-committee sources
   (Dovetail; ProductPlan) give is one decision-maker deciding on
   evidence. *(High.)*
2. **The role's scope is medium-neutral by definition, so CLI, API, and
   agent interfaces are inside it.** UX "encompasses all aspects of the
   end-user's interaction" (Norman & Nielsen); interaction design is "the
   conversation between the user and the system" (Cagan & Baxley 2025);
   SFIA's user-experience analysis skill (UNAN) covers "a full range of
   user tasks not just digital tasks". The CLI guidance corpus (clig.dev, Heroku, GitHub's
   Primer CLI) is design guidance in its own right — GitHub files its CLI
   design under its design system. *(High.)*
3. **What carries consistency across interaction types is not a
   component library — it is a small set of governed instruments:**
   design principles as decision rules (NN/g, GOV.UK's "consistent, not
   uniform"), one vocabulary and voice (Primer "Make it feel like GitHub";
   NN/g tone dimensions; the GOV.UK style guide), one core task set that
   every interaction type supports (NN/g omnichannel; Google's
   conversation design; Alexa "voice-first, but not voice-only"), an
   accessibility standard as a cross-cutting constraint (WCAG 2.2 AA;
   WCAG2ICT for non-web), and per-interaction-type conventions honoured
   as *external* consistency (NN/g usability heuristic 4, "consistency and standards"; clig.dev "the terminal's
   conventions are hardwired into our fingers"). Every mature example
   governs these with the same form: criteria + a review body + an
   approval state (GOV.UK contribution criteria; Google AIP editors;
   Azure's stewardship board). *(High.)*
4. **Conversational and agent interfaces have an established external
   check and a real paradigm difference.** Microsoft's 18 Guidelines for
   Human-AI Interaction are modality-independent; Google's conversation
   design rests on Grice's Cooperative Principle; Nielsen classes CLI and
   GUI together as command-based and conversational/agent as intent-based
   with "reversed locus of control", and expects hybrids. The designer's
   consistency task therefore spans two paradigms, and for generated
   interfaces the designer's output becomes "guidance and constraints",
   not screens. *(High for the guidance; medium for the paradigm claim,
   one author.)*
5. **The agent is also a user.** NN/g: "'user' is no longer synonymous
   with 'human'"; Anthropic: invest in the agent-computer interface "just
   as much effort" as HCI. Accessibility structure (semantic names,
   predictable patterns) and tool/API definitions are the agent's
   interface — so API/SDK ergonomics and agent tool contracts sit in the
   designer's consistency remit, with the architect owning the contract
   itself. *(High — two primary sources opened in full agree; both are
   recent, so the practice they describe is young.)*
6. **The contested boundary with the PM is known and must be allocated
   explicitly.** NN/g's 2021 survey: PMs and UX disagree most on who owns
   discovery research (19% of PMs vs 73% of UX say UX), ideation,
   information architecture, task flows, the research agenda, and who
   explains design to leadership. The recorded failure modes: PMs
   "dictate design by sending wireframes to product designers and asking
   them to polish them"; the designer as decorator ("pixel-pusher");
   hand-off leaving the designer to find requirement gaps. *(High.)*
7. **The proposal for `lead-product-designer`** — composed from findings
   1–6, a proposal not a finding, so no confidence label; written to the
   six-section role form used by `researcher` and
   `lead-solutions-architect` — posture; decision rights (decides,
   recommends, escalates, never decides); admissible evidence;
   interfaces; knowledge and skills; anti-rationalization. *Posture:* one experience across every
   interaction type; evidence from users, never opinion; consistent, not
   uniform. *Decides (exclusive domain):* the experience guidance corpus
   — design principles, vocabulary and voice, the core-task parity rule,
   interaction patterns per interaction type, the accessibility target —
   and whether a delivered interaction conforms to it. *Decides:* which
   interaction type a capability is offered through first — an
   experience call, since the PM has already decided the capability is
   worth having and the question left is how people reach it; the
   information architecture and task flows of every interaction type;
   what user research is run and how usability is evaluated. *Recommends:*
   to the PM, opportunities and usability findings that change value
   judgments; to the PO, acceptance scenarios' usability criteria and
   the scenarios that a usability test invalidates; to the architect, the
   ergonomics of contracts, CLIs, and agent tool definitions.
   *Escalates:* to the authority, a principle the experience corpus cannot
   satisfy alongside the architecture principles, and any conflict where
   value (PM) and usability pull apart after re-framing. *Never decides:*
   what problem is worth solving (PM), acceptance (PO), the stack and
   contracts (architect), how a Bounded Context builds a behavior (the
   shop). *Admissible evidence:* user tests and trials, prototypes tested
   with users, expert review against the corpus, context-of-use analysis,
   measured task completion; not admissible — a stakeholder's preference,
   a PM-supplied wireframe as a requirement, the designer's own taste
   unrecorded. *Interfaces:* PM — framed problems and outcomes in;
   usability findings, prototypes, and opportunity evidence out, in
   discovery not after it; PO — scenarios in for usability criteria;
   usability acceptance criteria and test results out; architect —
   contract, CLI, and tool ergonomics reviewed against the corpus;
   feasibility and non-functional constraints in; Bounded Context shops —
   the corpus and its patterns out; conformance findings back; a
   `clarify` on experience questions answered. *Knowledge and skills* and *anti-rationalization* are set out in full
   under "What this means" below.
8. **Two decisions the sources leave to the authority.** (a) Whether the
   experience guidance corpus is a new definition type or a principle
   set plus guidelines in the existing chain form — the governance
   examples fit the existing form. (b) Torres puts usability on the
   whole trio ("The trio is jointly responsible for building a
   desirable, viable, feasible, usable, ethical product"); Cagan on the
   designer alone; the proposal follows Cagan
   and RACI (one accountable) with joint discovery. *(Judgment.)*

## Method

Three parallel gather workers in fresh contexts covered: the role's
definition and interfaces (Cagan/SVPG six essays, Torres two, NN/g
seven, SFIA 9 four skills, practitioner sources on failure modes);
consistency mechanisms and CLI/API design (NN/g five, GOV.UK four,
Atlassian three, W3C two, clig.dev, Heroku, 12-factor CLI via mirror,
GitHub Primer CLI via repository source, Docker, Google AIP, Azure
guidelines, Stripe two, Textual — a terminal-UI framework's theming guide, the only
TUI design document found); conversational and agent interfaces
(Google conversation design three pages, Microsoft HAX, NN/g five,
Apple WWDC transcript, Alexa two, Google's People + AI Research (PAIR) guidebook two chapters, Shneiderman, Anthropic,
OpenAI). About 55 sources opened in full; unreadable: ISO 9241-210
(paywalled — principles from a secondary), Material Design 3
(JavaScript-rendered), NN/g "UX vs product designer", Apple HIG Siri
page (substituted by Apple's own WWDC20 transcript), Amershi et al. full
paper (abstract and Microsoft's library used), GOV.UK working-group page
(410; Home Office analogue opened). Evidence extracted quotes-first;
synthesis; an independent fresh-context verification pass followed.

## Findings

### F1 — The gap and its name *(high)*

- Cagan, "The Four Big Risks" (svpg.com/four-big-risks): "The Product
  Designer is responsible for the usability risk, and overall accountable
  for the product's experience – every interaction our users and
  customers have with our product." PM: "value and viability risks";
  engineer: "feasibility risk".
- Torres, "Core Concept: The Product Trio" (producttalk.org): "A product
  trio is typically comprised of a product manager, a designer, and a
  software engineer. These are the three roles that—at a minimum—are
  required to create good digital products."
- Torres, "Product Trios" (2024): "The trio is jointly responsible for
  building a desirable, viable, feasible, usable, ethical product."
- ProductPlan, "How to Avoid Design by Committee": "Design by committee
  is what happens when multiple parties are involved in the product
  design process, and all of their input is treated equally."
- Dovetail, "Design By Committee": "a group of designers, stakeholders,
  and clients working on the same project and sharing equally valid
  opinions"; "In product design, it usually produces low-quality
  results"; "you should only have one decision-maker". Riddle and
  Treder (UXPin), quoted by ProductPlan: "Committee design is not
  collaborative. It's a dictatorship of many".
- NN/g RACI (Kaley 2022): "For each task, there should be only one
  accountable person."
- Cagan 2006, on the absence: "Sometimes the product managers waded into
  the design waters and did what they could."

### F2 — Scope is medium-neutral *(high)*

- Norman & Nielsen, "The Definition of User Experience": "'User
  experience' encompasses all aspects of the end-user's interaction with
  the company, its services, and its products"; UX ⊃ UI ⊃ usability
  ("usability... is a quality attribute of the UI").
- Cagan & Baxley 2025: "The product designer is fundamentally responsible
  for the user experience of the product. The scope of that
  responsibility encompasses the full suite of interactions, touchpoints,
  and visual representations — both online and offline";
  "Interaction design is the practice of creating and choreographing the
  conversation between the user and the system."
- SFIA 9 UNAN: "This skill is inclusive of a full range of user tasks not
  just digital tasks."
- clig.dev: "If a command is going to be used primarily by humans, it
  should be designed for humans first"; "The original Macintosh Human
  Interface Guidelines recommend 'See-and-point (instead of
  remember-and-type)'... These things needn't be mutually exclusive."
- Heroku CLI style guide: "The primary goal of anyone developing CLI
  plugins should always be usability."
- GitHub Primer CLI (repository primer/cli, archived 2024, now under
  primer.style/design): "Command line interfaces are not as visually
  intuitive as graphical interfaces. They have very few affordances...
  We do our best to design our commands to mitigate this."
- Stripe (Bu 2020): "Keeping things simple means making sure your APIs
  are consistent and predictable"; "creating the right packages to
  gradually reveal the power of your API as your users need it."

### F3 — What carries consistency, and how it is governed *(high)*

- NN/g, Design Principles (Rosala): "Product design principles are value
  statements that describe the most important goals that a product or
  service should deliver for users and are used to frame design
  decisions."; "These principles support consistency in the way
  decisions are being made across teams, build confidence in the
  decision, and eliminate fruitless debates."; "Be careful that your
  principles don't conflict."
- GOV.UK Design Principles #9: "Be consistent, not uniform... We should
  use the same language and the same design patterns wherever possible.
  This isn't a straitjacket or a rule book." #7: "We're not designing for
  a screen, we're designing for people."
- NN/g heuristic 4: "Systems should adhere to both internal and external
  consistency — they should use the same patterns everywhere inside the
  system and should also follow web-, platform-, and domain-specific
  conventions." clig.dev: "The terminal's conventions are hardwired into
  our fingers... that's what makes CLIs intuitive and guessable".
- Primer CLI, "Make it feel like GitHub": "Using this tool, it should be
  obvious that it's GitHub and not anything else... reflect the
  GitHub.com interface as much as possible and appropriate"; "Language
  is the most important tool at our disposal for creating a clear,
  understandable product."
- NN/g tone of voice: "Keep your brand personality consistent, but vary
  the tone"; "used when creating writing and other communications for
  all channels."
- NN/g omnichannel: "Your channel experiences should at minimum support
  these core tasks on every channel"; "it's vital... to understand when
  it's okay to compromise consistency in order to provide an
  appropriately optimized experience on each channel."
- Atlassian: "Design tokens are the single source of truth to name and
  store decisions about the user interface."
- W3C: WCAG 2.2 "is an approved... ISO standard: ISO/IEC 40500:2025";
  "can also be applied to non-web information and communications
  technologies"; WCAG2ICT "is not a standard, so it is not possible to
  conform to WCAG2ICT".
- Governance form — GOV.UK contribution criteria: "tested in user
  research and shown to work with a representative sample of users,
  including those with disabilities"; "it has a clear owner". Google
  AIP-1: "Two AIP approvers (other than the author) must provide formal
  signoff"; AIPs "are used by API reviewers as a basis for review
  comments." Azure guidelines: "If you feel you need an exception,
  contact the Azure HTTP/REST Stewardship Board prior to
  implementation." NN/g Design Systems 101: "A design system is only as
  effective as the team that manages it."

### F4 — Conversational and agent interfaces *(high for guidance; medium for the paradigm claim)*

- Google conversation design (the pages carry a notice that
  "Conversational Actions were deprecated on June 13, 2023"; the design
  guidance outlives the retired product): "a breadth of design expertise (for
